anchor: MY Love is of a birth
title: The Definition of Love: title, date, form
short: A love lyric cast as a logical 'definition'; published posthumously in Miscellaneous Poems (1681), date of composition unknown.
body: In scholastic logic a definition states a thing's genus and its distinguishing difference; Marvell's poem defines a love whose essence is its impossibility, ending with a two-term formula ('Conjunction of the Mind, / And Opposition of the Stars'). It was first printed in Miscellaneous Poems (1681), issued after Marvell's death, and cannot be dated securely; editors usually place it with the lyrics of the late 1640s or early 1650s. The form is eight quatrains of iambic tetrameter rhymed abab, compact and epigrammatic. The poem's argument by geometry and astronomy has made it a classic example of 'metaphysical' wit, often compared with Donne's 'Valediction: Forbidding Mourning'.

title: begotten by despair / Upon Impossibility
short: An allegorical genealogy, parodying Plato's myth that Love was born of Resource and Poverty.
body: In Plato's Symposium (203b-c), Diotima tells how Eros was conceived by Poros (Resource) on Penia (Poverty) at Aphrodite's birthday feast, which explains love's needy yet resourceful nature. Marvell replaces the parents with Despair and Impossibility: the 'begetting upon' formula (the father begets upon the mother) gives a mock-scholastic precision. The love is 'rare' (unusual, precious) because its object is 'strange and high', too lofty to be attained.

title: Magnanimous Despair
short: Paradox: despair, usually abject, is 'great-souled', because only despair dares to contemplate so high an object.
body: Latin magnanimus, 'great-souled', translates Aristotle's megalopsychia, the virtue of the man who claims great things because he deserves them (Nicomachean Ethics 4.3). Hope, by contrast, is 'feeble' (l. 7): it calculates and so would never set out toward the impossible. The reversal of the usual moral values of hope and despair is the poem's first paradox. For a Christian reader despair was a sin, and the playful inversion is part of the poem's wit.

title: Tinsel Wing
short: Hope's wings are glittering but flimsy, like tinsel cloth, too weak to reach the beloved's height.
body: 'Tinsel' was a cloth interwoven with gold or silver thread, and by Marvell's time also meant anything showy but worthless (OED). Hope only 'flapt' its wings in vain, an undignified verb that makes it sound like a grounded bird. The image recalls Icarus and the Platonic winged soul (Phaedrus 246), but here flight is denied. Only despair, which expects nothing, can 'show' the divine object (l. 6); hope, which always expects some reward, is earthbound.

title: my extended Soul is fixt
short: The lover's soul is stretched out toward the beloved and fixed there, as if pinned at a point it cannot quite reach.
body: 'Extended' means stretched out, reaching; there may be a glance at the philosophical term for spatial extension, which made the soul seem paradoxically bodily. 'Fixt' suggests both steadfastness and a star fixed in its sphere, preparing the astronomical imagery of stanzas 5-8. The lover 'might quickly arrive' were it not for Fate. The word 'alwaies' (l. 12) makes Fate's interference perpetual, the first statement of the permanent separation that the geometry of later stanzas will prove.

title: Fate's Iron wedges
short: Fate drives iron wedges between the lovers; the image recalls Horace's Necessity carrying wedges in her bronze hand.
body: In Horace, Odes 1.35.17-20, Necessity goes before Fortune carrying nails, wedges, a clamp and molten lead, the tools of fixing and splitting. Editors cite the passage for Marvell's Fate. The wedge splits apart what would otherwise close, and 'crouds it self betwixt' makes Fate an intruder physically shouldering between the lovers. Marvell turns Horace's abstract Necessity into a jealous rival with a body and a will, and introduces the iron and steel ('Decrees of Steel', l. 17) that make Fate's rule unbreakable.

title: Fate's jealousy and tyranny
short: Fate keeps the lovers apart because their union would overthrow her rule; love and fate are cast as rival powers.
body: Fate is pictured as a jealous tyrant who fears that two 'perfect Loves' joined would make her 'ruine' and 'depose' her 'Tyrannick pow'r'. Some critics have heard the political vocabulary of the 1640s and 1650s (tyranny, deposition, decrees) in these lines; others take it simply as the conventional rivalry of Love and Fortune. 'Close' means unite, and also join in combat.

sources.cite: Nigel Smith, ed., The Poems of Andrew Marvell, rev. edn (Longman Annotated English Poets, 2007), note ad loc.

title: the distant Poles
short: The lovers are the North and South Poles: the whole world of love turns on them, yet they can never touch.
body: Fate's 'Decrees of Steel' fix the lovers like the earth's poles, the two ends of the axis around which the globe revolves. The parenthesis 'Though Loves whole World on us doth wheel' makes them the necessary centre of the universe of love while denying them contact. The image is a variant of the metaphysical cartographic conceit, compare Donne's 'Hymn to God my God, in my Sickness'.

sources.cite: Nigel Smith, ed., The Poems of Andrew Marvell, rev. edn (Longman Annotated English Poets, 2007), note ad loc.

title: Planisphere
short: A map projecting a sphere onto a flat surface; only if the globe were crushed flat could the two poles meet.
body: A planisphere is a representation of the celestial or terrestrial sphere on a plane. Only cosmic catastrophe could unite the lovers: the 'giddy' (whirling) heaven would have to fall, the earth be torn by 'some new Convulsion', and the world 'cramp'd' (squeezed) flat, so that the poles touched. Editors explain the geometry differently according to the type of projection they suppose, but the hyperbole is clear: the union is literally world-ending.

title: Lines oblique and parallel
short: Oblique lines meet at some angle; parallel lines, though extended infinitely, never meet, as Euclid defines them.
body: Euclid's Elements, Book I, definition 23, defines parallels as straight lines in the same plane which, produced indefinitely in both directions, do not meet. Ordinary loves are 'oblique', and so can 'greet' at an angle (with a pun on corners, angles, and on angling for advantage). The lovers' love is 'so truly Paralel' (exactly matched, equal) that it can never converge. 'Though infinite' applies to both the lines and the love.

title: Conjunction of the Mind, / And Opposition of the Stars
short: Astrological terms: the lovers' minds are 'in conjunction' (together), while their stars stand 'in opposition' (diametrically apart).
body: In astrology two planets are in conjunction when they occupy the same position in the zodiac, and in opposition when they are 180 degrees apart, the most hostile aspect. The final definition splits the love into its two terms: union of minds, and separation decreed by the heavens. The lovers are like opposed planets, which see each other face to face across the whole sky. 'Enviously' (l. 30) recalls the jealous Fate of stanza 4, and 'debarrs' means bars, shuts out.
